question: An administrator added a new user via mosquitto_passwd, but they can't connect. The broker is running. What's the problem?

options.text: The client needs to be restarted
options.explanation: No. The problem is on the broker side — it doesn't know about the new user. The client is not the issue.

options.text: The broker hasn't re-read the password file — needs kill -HUP or reload
options.explanation: Correct. Mosquitto reads the password file at startup and on SIGHUP signal. After modifying the passwd file: kill -HUP $(pgrep mosquitto) or /etc/init.d/mosquitto reload.

options.text: mosquitto_passwd creates a user with a locked account
options.explanation: No. mosquitto_passwd simply adds a record with a password hash. There are no locks.

options.text: The user needs to be added to the system's /etc/passwd
options.explanation: No. The system's /etc/passwd and /etc/mosquitto/passwd are different files. Mosquitto uses its own password file.

question: There's no ACL rule for topic 'device/sensor/data' for user 'sensor'. What happens on a publish attempt?

options.text: Access will be granted — denial must be explicit
options.explanation: No. Mosquitto ACL works on a 'whitelist' principle: explicitly allow what's needed. Everything else is denied.

options.text: The global rule for anonymous users will apply
options.explanation: No. The user is authenticated, so rules for their name apply. If there's no rule — access is denied.

options.text: Access will be denied — absence of a rule means deny
options.explanation: Correct. If an ACL file is set and there's no matching rule for the user and topic, access is denied by default (deny by default).

options.text: The broker will ask the administrator
options.explanation: No. The broker operates autonomously based on configured rules. There's no interactive authorization.

question: What does this line in the ACL file mean: pattern write devices/%c/data

options.text: Each client can publish only to a topic with its client_id
options.explanation: Correct. %c is replaced with the client_id of the connected client. Client 'esp32-01' can publish to devices/esp32-01/data but not to devices/esp32-02/data.

options.text: %c means controller
options.explanation: No. %c = client_id. %u = username.

options.text: The rule applies only to users with names starting with 'c'
options.explanation: No. %c is a special variable that is replaced with the client_id during access check.

options.text: All users can publish to any topic starting with devices/
options.explanation: No. %c is not a wildcard. It's a substitution of the specific client_id. Access is strictly to devices/{own_id}/data.

question: How does the Dynamic Security Plugin differ from password_file + ACL?

options.text: Supports user roles and groups
options.explanation: Yes. Dynamic Security introduces the concept of roles — sets of ACL rules assigned to multiple users. Changing a role changes the permissions of all users in that role.

options.text: Allows managing users via MQTT without restart
options.explanation: Yes. Management via $CONTROL/dynamic-security/v1 topics. No SIGHUP or restart needed.

options.text: Requires an external database (PostgreSQL, MySQL)
options.explanation: No. Dynamic Security Plugin stores data in a JSON file on disk. No external database needed.

options.text: Built into Mosquitto 2.x
options.explanation: Yes. Since Mosquitto 2.0, the Dynamic Security Plugin is part of the standard package.

question: Why does mosquitto-go-auth have 'limited support' on OpenWRT?

options.text: OpenWRT uses musl libc, while mosquitto-go-auth requires glibc (CGO incompatibility)
options.explanation: Correct. mosquitto-go-auth is written in Go with CGO. Compiled binaries are usually linked with glibc, while OpenWRT uses musl libc. Cross-compilation with musl is required.

options.text: OpenWRT doesn't have the go package for compilation
options.explanation: This is partially true (go is indeed not in opkg), but the main issue is libc incompatibility when running an already-compiled binary.

options.text: mosquitto-go-auth doesn't support MQTT v3.1.1
options.explanation: No. MQTT version compatibility is not the issue. The problem is with libc.

options.text: mosquitto-go-auth consumes too much RAM
options.explanation: RAM is a secondary issue. The main problem is the inability to run a glibc binary on a musl system.

question: The developer specified in mosquitto.conf: allow_anonymous true and password_file /etc/mosquitto/passwd. Can a client without login and password connect?

options.text: Depends on Mosquitto version
options.explanation: No. Behavior is the same for Mosquitto 1.x and 2.x: allow_anonymous is independent of password_file.

options.text: No — presence of password_file automatically denies anonymous users
options.explanation: No. password_file only adds the ability to verify passwords. To deny anonymous users, you need explicit allow_anonymous false.

options.text: Yes — allow_anonymous true permits anonymous connections despite password_file
options.explanation: Correct. allow_anonymous true and password_file don't conflict. An anonymous client connects via allow_anonymous. password_file is only checked for clients that PROVIDED credentials.

options.text: No — Mosquitto always requires authentication when password_file exists
options.explanation: No. Mosquitto only requires authentication when allow_anonymous is false.

question: Which mosquitto_passwd command flag RECREATES the file (deletes all existing users)?

options.text: -D (delete)
options.explanation: No. -D deletes a specific user from the file but doesn't recreate it.

options.text: -b (batch)
options.explanation: No. -b means batch mode: pass the password as a command-line argument. Doesn't recreate the file.

options.text: -c (create)
options.explanation: Correct. mosquitto_passwd -c /etc/mosquitto/passwd user creates a NEW file. If the file existed, it will be overwritten and all users lost!

options.text: -U (update)
options.explanation: No. There's no -U flag. Password update — call mosquitto_passwd again without -c for an existing user.

question: For an IoT system on OpenWRT with 100 sensors, you need to add new devices without restarting the broker. Which authentication mechanism to choose?

options.text: Dynamic Security Plugin (mosquitto_dynamic_security.so)
options.explanation: Correct. Dynamic Security Plugin is built into Mosquitto 2.x, supported on OpenWRT 23.x, requires no external dependencies, and allows managing users via MQTT without restart.

options.text: password_file + kill -HUP
options.explanation: kill -HUP allows re-reading the file without restart, but requires SSH access to the router. Dynamic Security Plugin is more convenient — management via MQTT.

options.text: JWT tokens
options.explanation: JWT requires additional implementation for token issuance. Harder to configure, no ready-made package for OpenWRT.

options.text: mosquitto-go-auth with Redis backend
options.explanation: Issues with musl libc on OpenWRT + additional dependency (Redis server). Excessive for an IoT router.
